cards.explanation: The answer is True, friends, and the text says it right out loud. The law covers a husband who suspects her, “…even though she has not defiled herself…” So the law looks at two situations, one where she has gone astray and one where she hasn't. Both start the same way, with a jealous husband and no witness. A hunch isn't a fact, and I once swore somebody swiped my last cookie when it was in my apron pocket the whole time.

The answer is the priest, friends. The text says the husband is to bring his wife to the priest. The priest then has her stand before the LORD, so the whole thing happens in front of Him and not in the husband's living room. Notice nobody is told to take it to a neighbor or settle it with a shouting match.

The answer is barley flour, friends. The text says a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. And no oil and no frankincense on top, which is a plain offering, like a cookie with no sprinkles. I love sprinkles, but this is the instruction the LORD gave.

The answer is dust from the tabernacle floor, bakers. The priest takes holy water in a clay jar and puts in some of the dust from the tabernacle floor. That's a very short ingredient list. My own recipes have more steps than that, and I still burn something every other Tuesday.

The answer is that the priest lets down her hair, friends. The text puts it right after she stands before the LORD and right before he places the grain offering in her hands. It's a quiet detail, and I won't guess what it means because the text doesn't say. I'll just say it's in there.

The answer is that the priest says, may she be immune to it. If no other man has slept with her, the priest says, “…may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse.” Verse 28 backs it up: if she is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. Immune, friends. That's the word on the page.

The answer is False, bakers. The priest says the words “then may the LORD make you an attested curse among your people by making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell.” The husband isn't the one named in that line. It's the LORD. This is one of the heavy parts, so it matters to get the words right.

The answer is “Amen, Amen.” That's the woman's whole answer after the priest speaks the curse over her (Numbers 5:22). One word, said twice. Sometimes the shortest line in the passage is the one that counts.

The answer is that the priest washes the curses off into the bitter water, friends. The priest writes the curses on a scroll and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). After that, he burns a handful of the grain offering on the altar, and then he has the woman drink the water (Numbers 5:26). I think this is a heavy part of the passage, so it's worth reading slowly.

The answer is False, bakers. The priest takes a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burns it on the altar (Numbers 5:26). He doesn't burn the whole offering, just the handful. It's a small detail, and it's worth noticing.

The answer is True, friends, and verse 28 says it. If the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. It's the other side of the curse in this law. The text gives both outcomes, and this one is the clean one.

The answer is priest, bakers. Verse 30 says the woman stands before the LORD, and the priest is to apply to her this entire law. He's the one all the way through, from bringing her forward to burning the handful on the altar. One person running the whole show is easier than three cooks and one oven.

The answer is that he will be free from guilt, friends. That's how the law closes about the husband, in verse 31. The next part of the verse is about the woman, and it's a heavy line. I think this is a part of the passage that's meant to be read slowly.
